UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.             )                      Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                )                      Docket No. EL25-49-001

                                   REPLY BRIEF OF
                       THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS

        Pursuant to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 order in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,

193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 193 (2025) (“Order”), the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners

(collectively, the “PJM Transmission Owners”)1 submit this reply brief to parties’ responses to the

initial briefs filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM Initial Brief”) and the PJM Transmission

Owners (“PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief”) on February 23, 2026 in the above-captioned

proceedings.




1
          For the purpose of this filing, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky
Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian
Transmission Company, AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, AEP Kentucky Transmission Company,
AEP Ohio Transmission Company, and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company; The Dayton Power and Light
Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a
Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy
Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its
affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company,
Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and
Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission
Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The
Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and
Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities
Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland
Electric Cooperative.
 I.      INTRODUCTION

        The PJM Transmission Owners’ proposals in this proceeding are grounded in two main

principles: (1) rates for the new services must be consistent with longstanding cost allocation

principles, and (2) the new services must be implemented in a manner that does not compromise

system reliability. Co-Located Load2 customers must pay their fair share of transmission system

costs, including those related to the benefits of being connected and synchronized with the

extensive PJM Transmission System. Otherwise, other ratepayers will be forced to subsidize Co-

Located Load customers. Additionally, reliability must be a key consideration of these new

services, not a secondary issue or afterthought. Co-Located Loads will be fully connected and

synchronized with the transmission system, and can have serious impacts on the system. The

laudable goals of promoting speed to power and economic efficiency for data centers and other

large load customers will not be well-served by implementing new transmission services in a

manner that results in significant risks and uncertainty around the ongoing reliability of the system.

Moreover, such a result risks undermining continued reliable service to existing customers.

        In this reply brief, the PJM Transmission Owners respond to a number of issues raised with

respect to PJM’s proposed non-rate terms and conditions for the three new transmission services

and their rate proposals for the new transmission services. The PJM Transmission Owners express

support for PJM’s proposed scope of the new transmission services, on the basis that they provide

reasonable flexibility to Co-Located Load customers while recognizing the need to implement

these new services in a reliable fashion. They also respond to criticisms of PJM’s proposed study

process, pointing out the important role that PJM Transmission Owners will continue to play with

respect to conducting load-related studies, and explaining why allegations of potential PJM

 Transmission Owner discrimination are without merit. The PJM Transmission Owners emphasize

the importance of PJM’s strong operational penalties given the potential for large amounts of load

to be secured from causing adverse system impacts based on the correct operation of control

technologies and protection systems and provide further detail on their proposal for

complementary financial penalties.

       The PJM Transmission Owners also address criticisms of their rate proposals for the new

transmission services. Specifically, the PJM Transmission Owners rebut claims that their proposal

to set the maximum rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service at the rate for Firm Contract

Demand Service is unjust and unreasonable, explaining the superiority of this service relative to

the existing Non-Firm Point-to-Point product and the need for further analysis prior to offering

any rate discounts. The PJM Transmission Owners further explain why their proposal for a Grid

Reliance Charge is just and reasonable and consistent with cost allocation principles, given the

benefits that the ongoing safe operation of the transmission system will provide to all Co-Located

Load, regardless of on-site generation.

II.    RESPONSE TO COMMENTS RELATED TO PJM’S PROPOSED TERMS AND
       CONDITIONS FOR THE NEW TRANSMISSION SERVICES

       A.      PJM has Appropriately Defined the Scope of Contract Demand and Interim
               Network Integration Transmission Services

       The PJM Transmission Owners support PJM’s proposals regarding the scope of Firm and

Non-Firm Contract Demand Services and Interim Network Integration Transmission Service

(“NITS”), including PJM’s proposal to restrict the use of Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to

periods when on-site generation is on outage.3 In particular, the PJM Transmission Owners agree

with PJM that Non-Firm Contract Demand Service is intended by the Commission to be a limited


3
       PJM Initial Brief, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al., Attachment B at P 17 (“Abdulsalam Affidavit”).



                                                      3
 service and is not a substitute for Firm Contract Demand Service or NITS for the portion of on-

site load that will not be served by on-site generation.

        Contrary to commenters’ assertions, there simply is no compelling reason for PJM not to

restrict Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to periods where a Co-Located generating facility is

on outage merely because the Commission did not limit the usage of Non-Firm Contract Demand

Service to outages.4 Nor do commenters provide a compelling basis for Non-Firm Contract

Demand Service to be available during non-outage conditions. In the Order, the Commission

explained that Non-Firm Contract Demand Service is intended to be an option for Eligible

Customers seeking to use the transmission system on behalf of Co-Located Load in a more limited

manner when on-site generation is not available to serve load.5

        Limiting the use of Non-Firm Contract Demand Service is also necessary to ensure the

reliable operation of the PJM transmission system, especially because PJM and the PJM

Transmission Owners will be relying on increased uses of Special Protection Schemes (“SPS”),

Remedial Action Schemes (“RAS”), and other control technologies and protective systems to

ensure that on-site load that is not being planned from a transmission expansion or capacity

standpoint can be operated reliably. As PJM witness Dr. Sami Abdulsalam explains in his affidavit

accompanying PJM’s Initial Brief, there are numerous operational and planning challenges

associated with implementing Non-Firm Contract Demand Service.6 For instance, transmission

 facilities serving large loads will likely have multiple feeders serving load, which will require

protection systems with multiple measurements, logics and significant flexibility, adding

complexity and reducing the reliability and overall security of the system.7 PJM witness Matthew

Wharton provides further details regarding the operational complexities associated with

implementing RASs.8 As Mr. Wharton explains, there is the possibility of interactions between

RAS in a tightly coupled network such as PJM, increasing the possibility of misoperations.9 Mr.

Wharton’s testimony details an incident where a failed lighting arrestor on a 230 kV transmission

system led to the loss of 1,500 MW within the PJM region at multiple substations, which highlights

the risk of having multiple RASs within a single area.10

       Given these risks and challenges, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service cannot become a

general substitute for firm service types such as NITS or Firm Contract Demand Service for load

that is not intended or designed to be served from on-site generation under normal (i.e., non-

outage) operating conditions. Instead, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service should be limited to a

supplemental service intended to provide as-available transmission capacity when such on-site

generation is on outage. This approach will properly balance flexibility for Co-Located Load

customers to obtain needed firm or non-firm service depending on their mix of on-site load and

generation, with the obligation to ensure that the system can continue to be operated reliably for

the benefit of all customers.

       In its Initial Brief and illustrative tariff records (“Illustrative Tariff”), PJM refers generally

to “outages” and being “on outage” without further explanation. PJM should clarify in any

“outage” is limited to periods where a generator is offline due to a breakdown or maintenance

issues, and does not cover other instances when a generator is not operating, such as when

intermittent generation resources are unable to produce; when a co-located battery has depleted its

available energy; or when a natural gas generator is unable to secure fuel.

        B.        PJM Appropriately did not Propose Changes to the Definition of Eligible
                  Customer

        In their comments, Invenergy Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC (together,

“Invenergy”) request clarification on how the Commission and PJM view the definition of Eligible

Customer in the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) when applied to the co-located

generator and co-located load.11 Specifically, whether a co-located generator would qualify as an

Eligible Customer on behalf of a Co-Located Load, and whether a co-located generator’s status as

an Eligible Customer depends on whether the co-location arrangement is in a jurisdiction that has

mandated retail choice.12

        In its Initial Brief, PJM appropriately proposed no changes to the definition of Eligible

Customer.      PJM’s definition of Eligible Customer is essentially identical to the definition

contained in the Commission’s pro forma Open Access Transmission Tariff. Under that definition,

an Eligible Customer can be an electric utility, a federal power marketing agency, or any person

generating electric energy for sale for resale (i.e., making wholesale sales), as well as a retail

customer taking unbundled transmission service pursuant to a state unbundling requirement.13 The

 answer to Invenergy’s questions would presumably depend on an individual co-located generator’s

specific factual circumstances. However, it seems unlikely that a co-located generator (as opposed

to the load) would meet the definition of an Eligible Customer for purposes of obtaining Contract

Demand Service. The generator likely would not be seeking to procure transmission service in

order for it to serve the on-site load, and instead would be selling its output directly to the on-site

load at retail (or to its state licensed supplier).14 The ability of a Co-Located Load, or an entity

representing the load, to qualify as an Eligible Customer would necessarily depend on whether the

jurisdiction in which it is located has adopted retail choice, and the related criteria adopted by the

state. This is because the Commission does not assert jurisdiction over bundled sales and under

Section 212(h), the Commission cannot mandate retail wheeling.15

         C.       The Commission Should not Mandate a Combined Interconnection and
                  Transmission Study Process for Co-Located Loads and Generation

         Invenergy argues that the Commission and PJM should clarify how transmission and

generator interconnection study processes can work in tandem.16 In Invenergy’s view, developers

and lenders will be reluctant to commit to projects without both sets of study results showing that

the project is viable and identifying expected upgrade costs, and coordinated studies would better

output of existing resources to serve new large loads at the expense of existing loads.

 align generation and load, improve efficiency, reduce system costs, and provide the certainty

needed for co-location projects to be financed and developed at scale.17

       It is unclear what Invenergy is asking for here, but to the extent it is requesting a combined

transmission and interconnection study process for Co-Located Load and generation, the

Commission should decline. PJM’s Initial Brief already sets forth a coordinated load and

generation study process, with the PJM Transmission Owners conducting load integration studies

and PJM performing generator interconnection and transmission service studies, when necessary.

As the PJM Transmission Owners explain in their March 25, 2026, joint response to PJM’s Initial

Brief, they are fully committed to continuing to work closely and collaboratively with PJM, as

they do today on numerous matters, to ensure that large loads can be quickly and efficiently

interconnected.18    In addition, the study process will be maximally efficient if the PJM

Transmission Owners conduct load integrating studies first to ensure that the load additions can

be reliably interconnected to the grid, which would then inform PJM’s generator interconnection

and transmission service studies.19 Conducting load integration studies first will help avoid

potential duplication of effort and expenses between PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners.20

       Furthermore, requiring PJM to adopt a single study process goes well beyond the issues set

for hearing by the Commission in the Order. PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners have

proposed a just and reasonable process for conducting the appropriate studies and ensuring they

are completed quickly and efficiently, consistent with the Commission’s directives in the Order.

 There is no reason for the Commission to entertain proposals that go beyond those directives, such

as requiring a single study process for Co-Located Loads.

       Moreover, regardless of the study process ultimately adopted by PJM, it cannot be ignored

or sidestepped that end-use load is still retail load and governed by existing load interconnection

rules set forth in state jurisdictional tariffs and agreements. There is no need for the Commission

to entangle itself in questions regarding the division between its jurisdiction over interstate

transmission matters and state jurisdiction over retail service in this proceeding. The coordinated

study approach proposed by PJM will provide a just and reasonable opportunity for Co-Located

Load to interconnect and assess the appropriate type and level of transmission service that the

customer wishes to obtain. The PJM Transmission Owners commit to continue working closely

with PJM to ensure the study process remains efficient and identifying any process improvements

needed to do so.

       D.       PJM’s Study Proposal Does not Promote Discrimination Against Co-Located
                Load Customers

       Certain commenters assert that PJM’s study procedures for the new transmission services

are too broad, lack detail, and do not address the terms and conditions for these new services with

sufficient detail, clarity or consistency.21 The same commenters contend that the study procedures

allow PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners too much discretion, which could result in delays

and undue discrimination.22

       While more detail regarding the study process for new transmission services, such as the

relevant steps in the process, associated timelines for studies, and study fees, may be helpful,

commenters’ concerns are overstated. This is particularly true with respect to accusations that the

 PJM Transmission Owners will use the study process to discriminate against Co-Located Load or

to deny co-location arrangements, or that references PJM Transmission Owner criteria as being

insufficient.23

         PJM’s Illustrative Tariff language appropriately provides that Transmission Owners will

play a key role in this study process. Transmission Owners will continue to have the responsibility

for performing load integration studies related to the interconnection of any new or modified Co-

Located Loads.24 Moreover, the design of any control technologies and protection systems will

need to be closely coordinated with Transmission Owners in order to ensure they meet both PJM

and PJM Transmission Owner criteria, as well as North American Electric Reliability Corporation

(“NERC”) requirements.25 Given these considerations, it is appropriate and sufficient only to

reference the need to incorporate each Transmission Owner’s related technical requirements in the

Tariff. Consistent with the Commission’s rule of reason,26 the Tariff need not include details of

each Transmission Owner’s requirements. The reference to studies conducted by the Transmission

Owners that PJM will consider inherently must refer to the studies Transmission Owners will

conduct in order to integrate load facilities. The PJM Transmission Owners do not, however,

oppose making this explicit in the Tariff.

are located. Vistra at 33.

        Claims that the PJM Transmission Owners will use their role in the study process and

“natural monopoly market power” to delay and deny co-location arrangements or otherwise

discriminate against Co-Located Load27 are baseless and speculative. Contrary to Constellation’s

assertions, there is no basis to simply assume that any PJM Transmission Owner would work to

frustrate the intent of Commission-accepted tariff provisions. Likewise, it is illogical that PJM

Transmission Owners would have an incentive, financial or otherwise, to discriminate against Co-

Located Loads in studying such arrangements, as any delay in implementing new Co-Located

Loads will simply mean fewer retail and transmission customers on the system to be served by

Transmission Owners. Likewise, it makes no sense that the PJM Transmission Owners would

eschew available tools, such as Co-Located Load arrangements, to the extent those arrangements

support their obligation to ensure grid reliability.

       E.       The PJM Transmission Owners’ Proposed Criteria Relating to Special
                Protection Schemes and Remedial Action Schemes are Just and Reasonable

       In their initial brief, the PJM Transmission Owners proposed criteria to help address the

potential adverse reliability impacts associated with a potentially substantial increase in reliance

on SPS/RAS and other protection systems resulting from implementation of the new transmission

services.28

       In its reply brief, Constellation states that it agrees with the PJM Transmission Owners that

all SPS and RAS should be fully redundant, as long as such redundancy is consistent with a two

circuit breaker in a series example that it provides in its reply brief.29 The PJM Transmission

Owners agree that the customer and Transmission Owner may own the circuit breaker(s) and

is unclear because typical substation construction does not necessarily mean that there will ever

only be two breakers in a series. The terminals formed by the circuit breakers on each end of the

conductors between a Transmission Owner’s and a customer’s facilities may be composed of one

or more than one circuit breaker. Regardless, it does not change the nature and design of the

protection systems used to accomplish SPS and RAS. The number of breakers will be determined

by the Transmission Owner’s and customer’s design practices and budget, and the Transmission

        Constellation also states that it “agrees in principle with the fourth recommendation”

to account for Co-Located Loads may be unavoidable due to technical characteristics of Co-

Located Load. However, to the extent new technical criteria in Manual 3, or any other manual,

make sense to apply more broadly to participants other than Co-Located Load, the PJM

Transmission Owners are amenable to that possibility. But PJM and the PJM Transmission

Owners should not be restricted from developing and implementing criteria applicable to Co-

Located Load as a class, if those criteria are based on reasonable technical differences between

        Relatedly, Vistra provides no convincing reason for the Commission to reject the PJM

Nevertheless, the PJM Transmission Owners recognize that to implement such limitations

appropriately, further details and guidelines need to be developed, and welcome further

engagement with stakeholders to assist PJM in doing so.

        F.       The PJM Transmission Owners Support PJM’s Proposed Operational
                 Penalties, and Provide Additional Details on Proposed Financial Penalties

                 1.        PJM’s Operational Penalties are Just and Reasonable

        The PJM Transmission Owners support the operational consequences and penalties

proposed by PJM that will apply to failures to follow load shedding/curtailment instructions and

control technology and protection system misoperation.38 Robust operational penalty provisions

are a necessary component of the new services because network upgrades are planned and built

only to accommodate load covered by Firm Contract Demand Service or NITS. Thus, it is crucial

these Co-Located Load arrangements likely will involve substantial amounts of load—hundreds,

        Constellation argues that PJM should simply adopt Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”)

High Impact Large Load (“HILL”) process, which imposes only financial penalties.41 This

argument is without merit. First, SPP’s HILL proposal differs in a several pertinent respects from

PJM’s proposal. For example, unlike SPP’s HILL proposal, under PJM’s proposal Co-Located

and protection systems.42 Under such circumstances, it is appropriate and necessary that PJM have

in place strong measures to ensure reliability and to incentivize customers to operate accordingly.

Moreover, PJM and SPP are two different regions with different characteristics, including

topology and proliferation of large loads.43              Financial penalties are proper but insufficient

safeguards against adverse operational consequences of the sort proposed by PJM.

 4   IV.   FINANCIAL PENALTY PROPOSAL

 5   Q.    Should unreserved use penalties apply to Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract

 6         Demand Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, or Interim NITS on behalf of

 7         Co-Located Load?

 8   A.    [Hammer] Yes. Robust penalty provisions are a necessary component of the new services

 9         required by the Commission. First, and most importantly, any penalties must be sufficient

10         to meaningfully deter Co-Located Load customers from exceeding their contract demand

11         or Interim NITS limits and making unreserved use of the transmission system. Because

12         network upgrades are planned and built only to accommodate load covered by Firm

13         Contract Demand Service or NITS, it is crucial that Co-Located Loads respect their

14         contractual limits, including any related curtailment or other instructions from PJM. This

15         concern is particularly acute because many of these arrangements will likely involve

16         substantial amounts of load—hundreds, if not thousands of MW—being served by on-site

17         generation but still connected to the grid. If these limits are not respected, the reliability

18         consequences to the system—and to existing customers that rely on the reliable operation

19         of that system—could be severe.

20   Q.    Has PJM proposed any penalties?

21   A.    [Hammer] Yes. PJM’s Initial Brief includes a table summarizing PJM’s proposed

22         operational penalties applicable to Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-
                                                                                          Exhibit No. PTO-0005
                                                                                                  Page 5 of 31

 1        Located Load.5 PJM explains that it also supports a financial penalty in addition to its

 2        proposed operational penalties and that it intends to work with the PJM Transmission

 3        Owners to explore a financial penalty framework.6 Specifically, PJM states that

 4        “[u]nreserved use penalties should apply to Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract

 5        Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, or

 6        Interim NITS on behalf of Co-Located Load.”7

 7                     The PJM Transmission Owners agree with PJM that the imposition of financial

 8        penalties is appropriate, as any penalty regime should rely on both operational

 9        consequences and complementary financial penalties. Although the PJM Transmission

10        Owners anticipate that operational penalties will provide the primary deterrent against

11        Eligible Customers serving Co-Located Load exceeding their reserved transmission

12        service use, financial penalties will play a valuable role in enhancing this deterrent as well

13        as ensuring the market and other ratepayers are made whole if an Eligible Customer serving

14        Co-Located Load exceeds its contract demand or Interim NITS limits.

15   Q.   Do the PJM Transmission Owners have a proposal for an appropriate penalty charge

16        to address any unreserved use of the PJM transmission system by an Eligible

17        Customer taking transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located load?

18   A.   [Hammer] Yes. In addition to PJM’s proposed operational penalties for failure to curtail

19        upon instruction, the PJM Transmission Owners propose to apply financial penalties in

20        instances in which an Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load

21        exceeds the authorized transmission service limits, as described in more detail below. The

 1        authorized transmission service limits will include any reduction based on curtailments

 2        directed by PJM.

 3   Q.   Do the PJM Transmission Owners propose that the Commission adopt a separate

 4        “Failure-to-Curtail” Financial Penalty?

 5   A.   [Hammer] No. The PJM Transmission Owners are not proposing that the Commission

 6        adopt a separate “failure‑to‑curtail” financial penalty. Instead, failure to curtail should be

 7        treated as a form of unreserved use and addressed through a single, unified unreserved use

 8        financial penalty framework. Failure to curtail inherently results in unauthorized use of the

 9        transmission system. As such, it is part of unreserved use and does not warrant a distinct

10        penalty mechanism. However, as indicated above, the financial penalties proposed here

11        will account for any failure to curtail by factoring any curtailments directed by PJM into

12        the determination of an Eligible Customer’s authorized transmission service limits.

13   Q.   Please describe the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed financial penalties for

14        unreserved use.

15   A.   [Hammer] The PJM Transmission Owners propose a financial penalty charge structure

16        for unreserved use with two components: (1) a base penalty charge, which applies to each

17        individual hour in which the reserved transmission service limit is exceeded, and (2) a

18        penalty ratchet, which applies when such exceedances occur repeatedly.

19   Q.   What is the base penalty charge?

20   A.   [Hammer] As described in more detail below, when an Eligible Customer taking service

21        on behalf of Co-Located Load exceeds its reserved transmission service limit, the base

22        penalty charge will be assessed for any hour in which at least one five-minute interval

23        occurs during which a customer’s telemetered load at the Point of Delivery exceeds its
                                                                             Exhibit No. PTO-0005
                                                                                     Page 7 of 31

 1        reserved transmission service limit. This five-minute interval is defined as an Exceedance

 2        Interval, and such an hour is defined as an Exceedance Hour. The base penalty charge will

 3        apply to each Exceedance Hour.

 4   Q.   What is the penalty rachet?

 5   A.   [Hammer] As described in more detail below, the penalty rachet applies when multiple

 6        Exceedance Hours occur during a particular time period. It is designed to discourage

 7        recurring reliance on unreserved transmission capacity. Under the penalty rachet

 8        framework, the penalty charges escalate as the frequency of unreserved transmission use

 9        increases. Specifically, if more than one Exceedance Hour occurs on the same calendar

10        day, an additional daily penalty applies. If exceedances occur on multiple calendar days

11        within the same calendar week, an additional weekly penalty applies. Likewise, if

12        exceedances occur in multiple calendar weeks within the same month, an additional

13        monthly penalty applies, and if exceedances occur in multiple months within the same year,

14        an additional yearly penalty applies. By progressively increasing the economic

15        consequences of repeated penalties, the penalty ratchet reinforces the expectation that

16        Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load customers manage their

17        load in a manner consistent with their reserved transmission service.

18        Base Penalty Charge

19   Q.   Please describe the base penalty charge in more detail.

20   A.   [Hammer] The base penalty charge will be assessed for any hour in which at least one

21        five-minute interval occurs during which a customer’s telemetered load at the Point of

22        Delivery exceeds its reserved transmission service limit. Such a five-minute interval is

23        defined as an Exceedance Interval, and such an hour is defined as an Exceedance Hour.
                                                                               Exhibit No. PTO-0005
                                                                                       Page 8 of 31

 1        The base penalty charge will apply to each Exceedance Hour. For purposes of determining

 2        whether one or more exceedances have occurred, each five-minute interval beginning with

 3        the first minute of each hour shall constitute a separate interval. Similarly, each hour from

 4        0100 through 2400 shall constitute a separate hour. I explain the calculation of the reserved

 5        transmission service limit and the base penalty charge in the following questions.

 6   Q.   How is the reserved transmission service limit determined?

 7   A.   [Hammer] For an Eligible Customer taking only Firm Contract Demand Service, the

 8        reserved transmission service limit will equal the Firm Contract Demand minus any

 9        curtailed MW. For an Eligible Customer taking only Non-Firm Contract Demand Service,

10        the reserved transmission service limit will equal the approved Non-Firm Contract Demand

11        minus any curtailed MW. For an Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand Service

12        and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, the reserved transmission service limit will equal

13        the Firm Contract Demand plus the approved Non-Firm Contract Demand minus any

14        curtailed MW. For an Eligible Customer taking Interim NITS, the reserved transmission

15        service limit will equal the Interim NITS demand minus any curtailed MW.

16   Q.   How is the base penalty charge applied to each Exceedance Hour?

17   A.   [Hammer] Under the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal, the base penalty charge will

18        be applied to each Exceedance Hour and will be calculated as:

19        Hourly Exceedance MW × Equivalent Hourly Firm Contract Demand (“FCD”) rate ×

20        number of Exceedance Intervals within the hour

21        Where:

22                Hourly Exceedance MW = Maximum telemetered load during the hour – Reserved

23        Transmission Service Limit for the hour
                                                                               Exhibit No. PTO-0005
                                                                                       Page 9 of 31

 1              Equivalent Hourly FCD rate = FCD rate / 8,760 hours

 2   Q.   Why is the Firm Contract Demand Rate used as the basis for assessing the penalty?

 3   A.   [Hammer] The Firm Contract Demand rate is used as the basis for assessing the penalty

 4        because, when a customer exceeds its reserved transmission service limit without

 5        authorization, the excess usage effectively imposes firm‑level demand on the system. In

 6        effect, the customer utilizes transmission facilities in the same manner as a firm load.

 7   Q.   Can you provide an example to illustrate the application of the base penalty charge

 8        concept?

 9   A.   [Hammer] Yes. The following example demonstrates the application of the base penalty

10        charge concept. This example is a hypothetical for illustration purposes only.

11        Firm Contract Demand (“FCD”) Rate is $72,000/MW-Year.
12
13              Equivalent Monthly FCD Rate: $6,000/MW-Month
14              Equivalent Weekly FCD Rate: $1,385/MW-Week
15              Equivalent Daily FCD Rate: $197.26/MW-Day
16              Equivalent Hourly FCD Rate: $8.22/MW-Hour
17
18        April 7, during Houring Ending (“HE”) 12:00 p.m., a Firm Contract Demand customer has
19        a total load of 500 MW and on-site generation of 400 MW. The customer has 100 MW
20        FCD and no approved Non-Firm Contract Demand for the hour.
21
22        At 11:17 a.m., the customer experiences a sudden trip of 400 MW of on‑site generation.
23        While internal power controls immediately begin ramping down load and transferring
24        supply to backup generation, there is a brief delay before the protection systems fully
25        respond. As a result, the customer draws approximately 300 MW from the transmission
26        system for a period of seven minutes, from 11:17 a.m. to 11:24 a.m. (i.e., spanning two
27        five-minute intervals (11:15-11:20 a.m. and 11:20-11:25 a.m.)).
28
29        Because the customer’s telemetered load exceeded its 100 MW of reserved transmission
30        service limit during the HE 12:00 p.m., the HE 12:00 p.m. qualifies as an Exceedance Hour,
31        triggering a financial penalty.
32
33        For HE 12:00 p.m.:
34             Maximum telemetered load = 300 MW
35             Reserved Transmission Service Limit = 100 MW
36             Hourly Exceedance MW = 300 MW – 100 MW = 200 MW
                                                                             Exhibit No. PTO-0005
                                                                                     Page 10 of 31

 1                  Hourly FCD Rate = $8.22/MW‑Hour
 2                  Number of Exceedance Intervals during the hour = 2
 3
 4        Base Penalty Charge for the HE 12:00 p.m.:
 5               = 200 MW × $8.22/MW‑Hour x 2
 6               = $3,288
 7
 8        This penalty charge is in addition to the customer’s existing obligation to pay for its 100
 9        MW of FCD under its transmission service agreement.
10
11        Penalty Ratchet

12   Q.   Please describe the penalty ratchet in more detail.

13   A.   [Hammer] The PJM Transmission Owners’ also propose a penalty ratchet to address

14        repeated exceedance behavior based on the frequency of unreserved use of the transmission

15        system. This penalty rachet is designed to discourage recurring reliance on unreserved

16        transmission capacity. Under this framework, the penalty rate escalates as the frequency of

17        unreserved transmission use increases. By progressively increasing the economic

18        consequences of repeated exceedances, the penalty ratchet reinforces the expectation that

19        Eligible Customers manage their Co-Located Load in a manner consistent with their

20        reserved transmission service limits.

21   Q.   Can you explain the overall mechanics of the penalty ratchet?

22   A.   [Hammer] Yes. The penalty ratchet is based on an Eligible Customer’s exceedance pattern

23        and applies escalating FCD–equivalent rates as the frequency of unreserved transmission

24        use increases. Depending on whether exceedances occur within the same calendar day,

25        calendar week, calendar month, or calendar year, the penalty ratchet applies daily, weekly,

26        monthly, or annual penalty charges, respectively. Below is an overview of the penalty

27        ratchet:

28

                                                                                         Page 11 of 31

                         Exceedance Pattern                           Penalty Rate Applied
          Multiple Exceedance Hours in a single calendar day        Daily FCD-Equivalent Rate
           Multiple Exceedance Days within a calendar week         Weekly FCD-Equivalent Rate
          Multiple Exceedance Weeks within a calendar month        Monthly FCD-Equivalent Rate
          Multiple Exceedance Months within a calendar year              FCD Annual Rate
 1
 2          Daily Penalty Charge
 3
 4   Q.     When does the Daily Penalty Charge apply, and how is it calculated?

 5   A.     [Hammer] The Daily Penalty Charge applies when multiple Exceedance Hours occur on

 6          the same calendar day. In that circumstance, the Daily Penalty Charge is calculated as:

 7          Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar day
 8          × Daily FCD-Equivalent Rate
 9          × Number of Exceedance Hours in the calendar day
10
11   Q.      Can you provide an example of the Daily Penalty Charge?

12   A.     [Hammer] Using the same example as in the base penalty charge section, assume the

13          customer exceeds its reserved transmission service limit in two separate hours on the same

14          calendar day (one exceedance at 10:30 a.m. and another at 11:15 p.m.). As I explained

15          above, each clock hour will be treated as a separate hour for purposes of this determination,

16          so even though these exceedances occurred within an hour of each other, they will be

17          treated as two Exceedance Hours. In that case:

18                Maximum Exceedance MW during the calendar day = 200 MW
19                Daily FCD Rate = $197.26/MW‑Day
20                Number of Exceedance Hours in the calendar day = 2
21

23
24          200 MW× $197.26/MW‑Day x 2
25               = $78,904
26
27          The Daily Penalty Charge is assessed in addition to the base penalty charge applicable to

28          each individual Exceedance Hour.

 2

 4   A.   [Hammer] The Weekly Penalty Charge applies when Exceedance Hours occur on multiple

 5        calendar days within the same calendar week. The Weekly Penalty Charge is calculated as:

 6        Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar week
 7        × Weekly FCD-Equivalent Rate
 8        × Number of Exceedance Days in the calendar week

 6        receives from a connection to the grid. These grid benefits include delivering ancillary

 7        services and a suite of essential reliability services, such as frequency support, inertia,

 8        voltage stability, fault current capability, ride-through and protection coordination,

 9        and providing sufficient short-circuit capability. As discussed above, the proposed Grid

10        Reliance Charge methodology results in a just and reasonable rate that appropriately

11        reflects the value of these benefits.

[Reserved]

                                   SCHEDULE [FCD]
                        Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service
                                  For Co-Located Load

1)     Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service in a Zone in which
Network Integration Transmission Service rates are determined based on formula rates set forth in
Attachment H shall pay a Monthly Demand Charge based on the Firm Contract Demand
Transmission Service Amount (MW), as specified in Eligible Customer’s Service Agreement,
which shall be determined as follows:

       MDC = FCDTSA X RTZ/12

       Where:

       MDC is the monthly demand charge

       FCDTSA is the Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service Amount (MW), as specified
       in Eligible Customer’s Service Agreement

       RTZ is the rate for Network Integration Transmission Service from Attachment H for the
       Zone in which the Eligible Customer’s Co-Located Load is located, stated in dollars per
       megawatt per year. For purposes of establishing the RTZ component in the relevant

Network Integration Transmission Service rates are not established based on formula rates shall
pay a Monthly Demand Charge based on the Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service Amount

or an Affiliate’s use) must occur solely by posting on OASIS, and (3) once a discount is negotiated,
details must be immediately posted on the OASIS. For any discount agreed to by Transmission
Provider, Transmission Provider must offer the same discounted transmission service rate for the

this Schedule and any other applicable charges, the Eligible Customer shall also pay any
Transmission Enhancement Charges for which it is designated as a Responsible Customer
under Schedule 12 appended to the Tariff based on the Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service Charges shall be credited to Eligible Customers taking Network Integration Transmission
Service, Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, and Firm Point-to-Point Transmission
Service based on each Eligible Customer’s pro rata share of the Zone’s annual peak load based on
the most recent 12-month period ending October 31. The Eligible Customer’s pro rata share shall
be based on the ratio of its Zone Network Load or Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service
Amount to the sum of Network Customer Loads in the Zone and Firm Contract Demand
Transmission Service Amounts for all Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract Demand
Transmission Service in the Zone, for the applicable peak period. The sum of these revenue credits
will appear as a reduction to the gross monthly rate for Firm Contract Demand Transmission
Service on a Eligible Customer’s bill in that month.

6)       Other Supporting Facilities and Taxes. In addition to the charges set forth in section (1)
of this schedule, the Eligible Customer shall pay charges determined on a case-by-case basis for
facilities necessary to provide Transmission Service at voltages lower than those shown
in Attachment H for the applicable Zone(s) and any amounts necessary to reimburse
the Transmission Provider for any amounts payable as sales, excise, “Btu,” carbon, value-added
or similar taxes (other than taxes based upon or measured by net income) with respect to the
amounts payable pursuant to the Tariff.
                                                                            Exhibit No. PTO-0006
                                                                                    Page 10 of 17

                                    SCHEDULE [GRC]
                                 Grid Reliance Charge for
                        Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service
                                   For Co-Located Load

Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service and Non-Firm Contract
Demand Transmission Service shall pay the Grid Reliance Charge for the Zone in which the Point
of Delivery for the Eligible Customer’s Co-Located Load is located.

1)      For Zones in which Transmission Owners in which the Network Integrated Transmission
Service charge is set pursuant to a formula rate, the Grid Reliance Charge shall be an annual charge
equal to the Zonal Grid Reliance Rate multiplied by the difference between the Eligible
Customer’s Co-Located Gross Demand and its Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service
Amount, both as specified in its service agreement for Firm Contract Demand Service. For those
Zones that include multiple Transmission Owners or Transmission Owners with multiple formula
rate revenue requirements that comprise the total Zonal Rate, the inputs from each relevant formula
rate revenue requirement and components thereof will be aggregated to determine the
Transmission Owners relevant expenses and costs used as inputs to the Zonal Grid Reliance Rate,
as set forth below.

For each such Zone, the Zonal Grid Reliance Rate shall be calculated as:

(The Zonal Network Integration Transmission Service Rate X the Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage
Allocator) X the Zonal Grid Reliance Demand Adjustment Ratio.

Where:

The Zonal Network Integration Transmission Service Rate shall equal the rate for Network
Integration Transmission Service set forth in Attachment H for the Zone with which the Co-
Located Load is interconnected, stated in dollars per megawatt per year.

The Grid Reliance Charge Fixed Percentage Allocator shall be calculated as follows:

         The Grid Reliance Charge Fixed Percentage Allocator shall be a percentage value
         calculated as the average of all TO GRC Revenue Requirement Percentages

         TO GRC Revenue Requirement Percentage = TO GRC Revenue Requirement / TO Net
         Revenue Requirement

         TO GRC Revenue Requirement = [TO GRC Transmission O&M Percentage X TO
         Transmission O&M Expense] + [TO GRC Depreciation Expense]

         The TO GRC Transmission O&M Percentage shall be determined for each Transmission
         Owner in PJM for which FERC Form No. 1 account-level data is publicly available, and
         shall be equal to the amounts in FERC accounts 561-564 and 570-572 set forth in the
         Transmission Owner’s most recently published FERC Form No. 1, divided by the
                                                                              Exhibit No. PTO-0006
                                                                                      Page 11 of 17

       Transmission Owner’s transmission operations and maintenance amount contained in its
       most recently published FERC Form No. 1.

       The TO GRC Transmission O&M Expense shall be determined for each Transmission
       Owner in PJM, and is equal to the transmission operations and maintenance expense
       portion of the Transmission Owner’s revenue requirement determined based on its
       Attachment H formula rate template, as published in its most recent annual update.

       The TO GRC Depreciation Expense shall be determined for each Transmission Owner in
       PJM and shall be equal to the transmission depreciation expense portion of the
       Transmission Owner’s revenue requirement determined based on its Attachment H formula
       rate template, as published in its most recent annual update.

       The TO GRC Revenue Requirement Percentage shall be determined for each Transmission
       Owner in PJM and shall be equal to the Transmission Owner’s GRC Revenue Requirement
       divided by the Transmission Owner’s net transmission revenue requirement determined
       based on its Attachment H formula rate template, as published in its most recent annual
       update.

The Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator shall initially be calculated as of the effective date
of this Schedule, and will be published on the Transmission Provider’s website.

The Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator will be updated by the Transmission Provider
beginning with the first January 1 falling after the fifth anniversary of the effective date and every
subsequent fifth anniversary of the most recent update thereafter. No later than November 1 prior
to the update effective date, each Transmission Owner will provide to the Transmission Provider
the information required to determine the Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator. No later than
the following December 1, the Transmission Provider shall post on its website and in an
information filing with FERC, the updated Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator including
the information used to determine the Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator. The updated
Grid Reliance Charge for each Transmission Owner will become effective on the same date that
its Network Integrated Transmission Service Charge is updated in the year following the update
of the Grid Reliance Fixed Percentage Allocator.

The Zonal Grid Reliance Demand Adjustment Ratio shall be calculated as the ratio of the Zonal
demand used to determine Network Integration Transmission Service and Firm Contract Demand
Transmission Service rates to the sum of this Zonal demand amount plus the Co-Located Gross
Demand in excess of Firm Contract Demand for all Co-Located Load being served by Firm
Contract Demand Transmission Service in the Zone.

2)      For Zones in which Transmission Owners charge for Network Integrated Transmission
Service is not based on a formula rate, the Grid Reliance Charge shall be specified in a separate
rate schedule to be filed by the Zonal Transmission Owner and to be effective on the same date as
this Schedule [GRC] and updated each time such Transmission Owner updates its Network
Integrated Transmission Service charge.

                                                                                   Page 12 of 17

3)      Revenues collected from Grid Reliance Charges shall be credited to Eligible Customers
taking Network Integration Transmission Service, Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service,
and Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service, based on each Eligible Customer’s pro rata share
of the Zone’s annual peak load from the most recent 12-month period ending October 31. The
sum of these revenue credits will appear as a reduction to the gross monthly rate for service on an
Eligible Customer’s bill in that month.
                                                                            Exhibit No. PTO-0006
                                                                                    Page 13 of 17

                                     SCHEDULE [FP]
                                Financial Penalty Charge for
                             Unreserved Use by Co-Located Load

An Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract
Demand Transmission Service, or Interim Network Integration Transmission Service on behalf of
Co-Located Load shall be subject to financial penalties for its unreserved use of the transmission
system.

The financial penalty charge for unreserved use shall include two components: (1) a base penalty
charge, which applies to each individual hour in which the reserved transmission service limit is
exceeded, and (2) a penalty ratchet, which applies when such exceedances occur repeatedly.

Base Penalty Charge

When an Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load exceeds its reserved
transmission service limit, a base penalty charge shall be assessed for any hour in which at least
one five-minute interval occurs during which the Eligible Customer’s telemetered load at the Point
of Delivery exceeds its reserved transmission service limit. This five-minute interval is defined as
an Exceedance Interval, and such an hour is defined as an Exceedance Hour. The base penalty
charge shall apply to each Exceedance Hour.

       For an Eligible Customer taking only Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, the
       reserved transmission service limit shall equal the Firm Contract Demand Transmission
       Service minus any curtailed MW.

       For an Eligible Customer taking only Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service,
       the reserved transmission service limit shall equal the approved Non-Firm Contract
       Demand Transmission Service minus any curtailed MW.

       For an Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand
       Transmission Services, the reserved transmission service limit shall equal the Firm
       Contract Demand Transmission Service plus the approved Non-Firm Contract Demand
       Transmission Service minus any curtailed MW.

       For an Eligible Customer taking Interim Network Integration Transmission Service, the
       reserved transmission service limit shall equal the Interim Network Integration
       Transmission Service demand minus any curtailed MW.

       Each five-minute interval beginning with the first minute of each hour shall constitute a
       separate interval and each hour from 0100 through 2400 shall constitute a separate hour for
       purposes of determining whether one or more exceedances have occurred.
                                                                           Exhibit No. PTO-0006
                                                                                   Page 14 of 17

The base penalty charge shall be applied to each Exceedance Hour and shall be calculated as:

       Hourly Exceedance MW × Equivalent Hourly Firm Contract Demand (“FCD”) rate ×
       number of Exceedance Intervals within the hour

       Where:

             Hourly Exceedance MW = Maximum telemetered load during the hour – Reserved
       Transmission Service Limit for the hour

                Equivalent Hourly FCD rate = FCD rate / 8,760 hours

Penalty Ratchet

A penalty rachet shall apply when multiple Exceedance Hours occur during a particular time period
in order to escalate the penalty charges as the frequency of unreserved transmission use increases.

       If more than one Exceedance Hour occurs on the same calendar day, an additional daily
       penalty shall apply.

       If exceedances occur on multiple calendar days within the same calendar week, an
       additional weekly penalty shall apply.

       If exceedances occur in multiple calendar weeks within the same calendar month, an
       additional monthly penalty shall apply.

       If exceedances occur in multiple calendar months within the same calendar year, an
       additional yearly penalty shall apply.

The penalty ratchet shall be based on an Eligible Customer’s exceedance pattern and applies
escalating FCD-equivalent rates as the frequency of unreserved transmission use increases.
Depending on whether exceedances occur within the same calendar day, calendar week, calendar
month, or calendar year, the penalty ratchet shall apply daily, weekly, monthly, or annual penalty
charges, respectively, as follows:

Exceedance Pattern                                          Penalty Rate Applied
Multiple Exceedance Hours in a single calendar day          Daily FCD-Equivalent Rate
Multiple Exceedance Days within a calendar week             Weekly FCD-Equivalent Rate
Multiple Exceedance Weeks within a calendar month           Monthly FCD-Equivalent Rate
Multiple Exceedance Months within a calendar year           FCD Annual Rate

Daily Penalty Charge
The Daily Penalty Charge is calculated as:
       Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar day
       × Daily FCD Equivalent Rate
       × Number of Exceedance Hours in the calendar day
                                                                         Exhibit No. PTO-0006
                                                                                 Page 15 of 17

Weekly Penalty Charge
The Weekly Penalty Charge is calculated as:
      Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar week
      × Weekly FCD Equivalent Rate
      × Number of Exceedance Days in the calendar week

Monthly Penalty Charge
The Monthly Penalty Charge is calculated as:
      Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar month
      × Monthly FCD Equivalent Rate
      × Number of Exceedance Weeks in the calendar month

Annual Penalty Charge
The Annual Penalty Charge is calculated as:
      Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar year
      × Annual FCD Rate
      × Number of Exceedance Months in the calendar year
